Resettlement · Kenya

Dated structure records for compulsory acquisition and resettlement

Kenyan law values compensation at the date of the notice of intention to acquire, compensates occupants in good faith for improvements made before the Gazette notice, and requires land to be acquired to be geo-referenced. Lender standards ask for a census and a cut-off date. AfriScan maps the structures that existed on a given date, and what has appeared since, from dated imagery, so your census team knows where to look and your records show what was there. We count structures, not people; eligibility is decided by the acquiring body, the National Land Commission and your resettlement action plan.

Used in: Oil & gas · Power & utilities · Rail & roads · Mining · Project finance & ESIA

Request a proposal The dates that matter

What the rules ask for

The Land Act, the National Land Commission and lender standards

Compulsory acquisition under the Land Act

Compulsory acquisition runs under Part VIII of the Land Act 2012 (sections 107–133), through the National Land Commission. Its rules tie compensation to dates:

  • “Full” compensation restores the value of the land and its improvements “as at the date of the notice of intention to acquire the land” (s.2), and applies to compulsory acquisition and to the creation of wayleaves, easements and public rights of way.
  • “Prompt” means within a reasonable time and in any case not more than one year after taking possession (s.2).
  • Occupants in good faith without title are compensated on six years’ uninterrupted occupation immediately before the notice of intention is published, and for improvements made before its publication in the Gazette (s.107A(9)).
  • Geo-referencing: “All land to be compulsorily acquired shall be geo-referenced and authenticated” by the survey authority (s.107(8)).
  • Lapse: an acquisition not completed within 24 months of the notice of intention lapses (s.111(1B)).
  • Disputes go first to the Land Acquisition Tribunal (s.133C(6)), then to the Environment and Land Court.
  • Taking possession must not leave people homeless (s.120(1)).

Resettlement plans and lenders

We found no standalone resettlement statute in Kenya. Resettlement rests on the Land Act, on the Mining Act’s rule that people who prefer to be compensated by resettlement are settled on suitable alternative land at the licence holder’s cost (s.153(8)–(9)), and on lender standards such as IFC Performance Standard 5 and the World Bank’s ESS5, which ask for a census and a cut-off date.

Published resettlement action plans for transmission lines define the cut-off date as the completion of the census and asset inventory, and provide for re-ratifying it by Gazette notice after a delay of two years or more. Some of those dates were fixed years before construction. See power-line wayleaves.

What a dated register supports

A dated, reproducible record of the structures in the footprint shows what stood where on the date that matters. It supports your census and asset inventory, your notices and your IFC Performance Standard 5 cut-off-date records. It does not set any date, value any improvement or replace the census.

A summary for orientation as of 27 September 2026, not legal advice. The wayleave law guide has the procedure in full.

The dates that matter

One footprint, several dates, one register

s.107A(9)(a)

Six years before the notice

Which structures stood at each location on imagery from the start of the six-year period, where archive imagery exists. Occupation itself stays with the census.

s.2, valuation date

The notice of intention

The structures in the footprint on imagery as close as possible to the notice date, the date “full” compensation is valued at.

s.107A(9)(b)

The Gazette notice

Improvements made before the notice was published in the Gazette count; the register shows which structures appear on imagery from before that date.

RAP

The cut-off date

The structures on imagery closest to the completion of the census and asset inventory, or to a re-ratified date where the plan has been delayed.

s.111(1B)

The 24-month mark

An acquisition not completed within 24 months of the notice lapses, so a baseline made at the notice may need a fresh one if the process starts again.

Change

Since then

New structures since any of those dates, flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, and a location check of every dated image for a single grievance or claim.

A structure can only be dated between two images: the last one that does not show it and the first one that does. The record is as precise as the imagery on either side of the date, and the proposal says which dated scenes exist for your footprint before you commit.

How it works

Before the census, on the date, and after

Before the census. How many structures stand in the footprint and the buffers around it, and where they cluster, so the census and asset-inventory teams are sized and routed before they go. On a long wayleave, the busiest 500 m segments come first.

On the date. A register of the structures on dated imagery, with IDs, coordinates and reviewer categories such as main building, outbuilding, livestock enclosure or under construction. Categories describe what the imagery shows; use, occupancy and value are for your census, and compensation needs verification on the ground. Where the record may be tested later, it is packaged as an evidence pack with file fingerprints and an independent timestamp.

After. Repeat scans of the footprint and any resettlement site, with new structures since the cut-off date flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, and a location check for single grievances and claims: every dated image covering one point, on one sheet.

The imagery. A cut-off record is only as good as the date on its imagery, so we build it on imagery with a known capture date: a dated very-high-resolution satellite scene, a drone survey flown with the approvals each job requires, or georeferenced imagery you already hold. Map-service basemaps, which carry no capture date, are never used for it. A new satellite capture can be requested when the archive is too old; its date depends on satellite availability and weather and is never guaranteed.

What you receive

  • A structure register: ID, coordinates, category and imagery date
  • Maps of the footprint and buffers
  • A PDF report in English
  • GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers
  • An evidence pack with file fingerprints and an independent timestamp
  • Change layers and a notice after each repeat scan

Who uses it

Acquiring bodies, their consultants, and the people who check their work

Acquiring bodies and land teams

At pipeline, power, road, rail and mining projects, preparing notices, planning the census and keeping the dated record the Land Act turns on.

ESIA and RAP consultants

Fast, dated structure counts to size a census and asset inventory, compare route options and check the field inventory, in the formats their teams already use.

Lenders and independent monitors

Checking between site visits what has changed in the footprint and at resettlement sites since the cut-off date.

Limits

What a dated register is not

What it supports

  • Census and asset-inventory planning
  • Notices to occupiers along a wayleave (Land Act s.144(4))
  • Your IFC Performance Standard 5 cut-off-date records
  • Grievance handling and tribunal cases, with dated facts
  • Comparison of route and site options before a notice is issued

What it does not do

  • Set a notice, Gazette or cut-off date, or decide who is eligible
  • Carry out the census, the asset inventory or public participation
  • Value land, structures, crops or trees
  • Identify households or people, or show occupation
  • Replace the survey authority’s geo-referencing and authentication

Frequently asked questions

Does the imagery set the cut-off date?

No. In the resettlement action plans we have read, the cut-off date is the completion of the census and asset inventory, and a delay of two years or more can see it re-ratified by Gazette notice. Our register records what stood in the footprint on the dates you name; it supports the cut-off-date record rather than defining it.

Can imagery show six years' occupation?

Not occupation. Imagery can show whether a structure stood at a location on each dated image across the period, where such images exist. Who occupied it, and in what capacity, is for the census, the acquiring body and the National Land Commission. The Land Act compensates occupants in good faith without title on six years’ uninterrupted occupation before the notice of intention, and for improvements made before its Gazette publication (s.107A(9)).

Can the register be used before the Land Acquisition Tribunal?

It can support a case as a dated, located record of what stood where. Compulsory acquisition and wayleave disputes go first to the Land Acquisition Tribunal (Land Act s.133C(6)). Where you need to show that the files have not changed since delivery, an evidence pack adds file fingerprints and an independent timestamp. How a record is used in a dispute is for your counsel.

Does your GIS output meet the geo-referencing requirement?

It supports it. The Land Act requires land to be compulsorily acquired to be “geo-referenced and authenticated” by the survey authority (s.107(8)). Our layers carry coordinates for each structure and the footprint you give us, which your surveyors can use; the authentication stays with the survey authority.

Do you identify households or occupants?

No. We map structures, not people, and the register carries no names. Personal data from the census stays in your census; see data protection and aerial mapping.

Setting a notice or cut-off date?

Tell us the footprint or wayleave, the counties, the census window and the dates the record must reflect. We reply with the dated imagery that exists for them and a written proposal.
